rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 1-2 report the authors' own field experiments on four sod fields in North Carolina (2018) comparing a UAV mapping-plus-spraying system with ground broadcast applications.
rows.notes: The study does not measure crop productivity, yield or any sustainability outcome. It shows that UAV weed maps used to direct a UAV sprayer reduced treated area by 20-60% relative to broadcast (Tables 1-2) and documents weed injury; it also notes that mapping was repeated at 14 and 28 DAT. These are preconditions/related efficiency results, not evidence that UAV weed surveillance enhances crop productivity. Function of the claim (crop_production) is not addressed.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, Tables 1-2: own randomized complete block field trials in two locations. Q2: Section 2.2-2.3 and Tables 1-2: UAV orthomosaic weed maps (0.82 cm/pixel) were used to generate prescription flight paths for a UAV sprayer; the UAV-IS treated 77% vs 98% (natural weeds) and 33% vs 93% (surrogate weeds) of plot area, treated far less non-weedy area (30% vs 92% false positives), and achieved measured weed injury (Table 1: 81% K. striata injury; Table 2: 85-94% tobacco injury), i.e. map-guided precision application reduced herbicide-treated area and off-target coverage while controlling weeds. Q4: Section 2.4 and Tables 1-2: the intermediate variables (area sprayed, true/false positives, precision, recall, application efficiency) through which maps reduce chemical input were quantified per plot. Q7: Section 3.2 and 3.4/Conclusion: authors state efficiency gains occur where weed distribution is clearly aggregated (patchy) and that efficacy impact depends on weed distribution and morphology; application efficiency tripled only under highly aggregated surrogate weeds. Q8: Section 3.3 and 3.4/Conclusion: UAV sprayer deviated up to 1 m from target due to GPS accuracy without RTK; UAV-IS missed up to 26% of target weedy area; flight-path criteria acknowledged as arbitrary; payload/battery limits noted; risk of weed seed production from missed patches; technology requires several software/technical steps.
rows.notes: Claim elements not tested: operational costs were not measured, mechanical control was not evaluated, and only herbicide area/off-target coverage (not environmental impact per se) was quantified. Q3: injury maps were ground-verified and tobacco dry weight was measured, but the chemical-reduction result (area sprayed) rests on one image-overlay method; counted as no. Q5: two locations/soils and two weed systems only. Q6: plots of 100-136 m2. Q9: tables give means and P values only, no SD/SE/CI.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a primary field experiment integrating UAV RGB imagery weed mapping with an autonomous UAV sprayer in turf sod fields; no crop yield or cost data.
